title: A Student's Daring Projection Brought the Cinerama Dome Back from the Dead
summary:
For years, the Cinerama Dome sat dark, a ghost of Hollywood's golden age. Its curved, 86-foot-wide screen—once the ultimate canvas for 70mm epics—had been silent since the pandemic shuttered the ArcLight complex in 2020. Then, in March 2026, a 26-year-old film student named Ben Steinberg committed an act of guerrilla activism: he projected the faces of the theater's owners, the Decurion Corporation, onto the Dome's facade. The bold move risked a citation, but it also caught the eye of Sony Pictures.

Steinberg had been fighting for the Dome since 2021, launching a Twitter account and an online petition that eventually gathered over 30,000 signatures. His campaign, Save Your Cinema, tapped into a deep well of Los Angeles nostalgia and cinephile frustration. The Dome wasn't just a building; it was a landmark where generations experienced films on a scale that felt almost sacred.

Sony's purchase and the announcement that Alamo Drafthouse will operate the venue mark a stunning victory for grassroots advocacy. The adjacent multiplex, once a temple for 70mm presentations, will also reopen. On IndieWire's "Screen Talk" podcast, Steinberg revealed his next target: the Bruin Theater in Westwood Village, a 90-year-old movie palace that has fallen into disrepair. His organization is now expanding, aiming to rescue other historic cinemas.

Steinberg's story is a reminder that passionate individuals can still shift the course of cultural preservation. As he put it, sometimes you have to project your message—literally—to make the world see what's at stake.
why_it_matters: This victory shows that cultural landmarks aren’t just buildings — they hold shared memories and identity, and young activists can force powerful corporations to listen. It raises the question of what public spaces we value and how far we’re willing to fight to keep them alive for the future.

background_read: The Cinerama Dome opened in 1963 on Sunset Boulevard in Hollywood as a showcase for Cinerama, an early widescreen format that used three synchronized projectors to create an immersive image on a deeply curved screen. Over the decades it became part of the ArcLight multiplex, beloved for its high-quality projection and strict no-talking policy. Its geodesic‑dome design earned it status as a Los Angeles Historic-Cultural Monument.

When the COVID-19 pandemic forced theaters to close in 2020, the parent company Decurion Corporation (a real estate firm that owned the Hollywood complex) decided it would not reopen the ArcLight venues, including the Dome. The decision sparked intense outcry, and Ben Steinberg’s Save Your Cinema campaign tapped into that frustration — using a guerrilla light projection to catch the attention of Sony Pictures (one of the major Hollywood studios). Sony’s purchase and partnership with Alamo Drafthouse (a dine‑in chain known for cult films and strict no‑texting rules) represents a rare win for preservationists during an era when many historic cinemas are being turned into retail or luxury apartments.

perspectives.description: The reopening of the Cinerama Dome is a morale boost for Los Angeles’s film culture and a model for how grassroots pressure can reverse corporate decisions. It brings back a unique moviegoing experience — curved screen, 70mm projection — that streaming cannot replicate, and creates jobs for theater workers.

Some preservationists worry that the Dome’s rescue comes at the cost of being absorbed into a corporate chain like Alamo Drafthouse, which may commercialize what was once an independent shrine to cinema. Others point out that not all historic theaters can attract a Sony-size savior, and many equally important venues remain in disrepair without a Ben Steinberg to champion them.

perspectives.perspective: Neutral / Analytical (Historic Theater Preservation in the Streaming Age)
perspectives.description: The Cinerama Dome’s story mirrors a national struggle: hundreds of classic single-screen and multiplex theaters have closed since 2000, as audiences shift to on-demand viewing. Adaptive reuse — turning old cinemas into live entertainment venues or art spaces — is one path, but purists argue that losing the original function erodes film history. Steinberg’s campaign suggests nostalgia still has market power, but it requires creative, sometimes illegal, tactics to be heard.

If Save Your Cinema succeeds with the Bruin Theater, it could spawn a wave of Gen‑Z-led preservation campaigns in other cities. The challenge is scaling this model: not every historic venue has a photogenic dome or a dedicated student willing to risk arrest. The long-term question is whether corporate partnerships can be balanced with community ownership, ensuring these spaces remain accessible and not just luxury experiences.
